title: Mains electricity — AC, DC and your home's wiring
examTip: Favourite exam questions: wire colours, what each wire does, and why earth + fuse work together. Learn them by heart.
introTips: Before reading, try to recall the colour and job of each wire in a three-pin plug. Check your answers as you go.
Sketch an oscilloscope trace for both AC and DC from memory. Then look at the real thing to compare.
Think about every appliance at home with a plastic casing. Why doesn't it need an earth wire?
intro: When you plug in a kettle, charge your phone or switch on a light, you use a carefully designed system. It keeps you safe from voltages that could kill. The UK mains supply gives 230 V of alternating current. That is enough to kill. Yet people use it millions of times a day without harm. That safety comes from smart engineering. It uses the right wires in the right colours, and fuses that melt before fires start. Earth connections also drain dangerous current away from you.

keyPoints.heading: AC vs DC
keyPoints.content: Direct current (DC): current flows in one direction only. The voltage is constant. It comes from cells, batteries and solar panels. It is used in phones, laptops and torches. Alternating current (AC): the current keeps reversing direction. It alternates back and forth. The UK mains supply is AC at 230 V and 50 Hz (50 complete cycles per second). The frequency is 50 Hz. So the current reverses direction 100 times every second. Why do we use AC for mains? Transformers only work with AC. They cannot step DC voltages up or down. The National Grid uses high voltages (up to 400,000 V) to send electricity across the country efficiently. Transformers change the voltage at each end. This is only possible with AC. On an oscilloscope, DC shows as a flat horizontal line. AC shows as a sinusoidal wave: a smooth, repeating S-curve with equal peaks and troughs. The peak voltage is higher than the stated 230 V. The 230 V is the root mean square (RMS) value. This is the DC voltage that would give the same power.
writeBullets: DC — current in one direction only. Constant voltage. Comes from batteries and cells
AC — current keeps reversing direction. Comes from the mains supply
UK mains: 230 V, 50 Hz (50 cycles per second)
AC is used for mains because transformers need AC. They allow efficient high-voltage transmission
Oscilloscope: DC = flat line; AC = sinusoidal wave
230 V is the RMS value. The peak voltage is higher (~325 V)

keyTerms.def: Current that flows in one direction only, with constant voltage. Produced by batteries and cells.
Current that repeatedly reverses direction. The UK mains is AC at 230 V, 50 Hz.
The number of complete AC cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz). UK mains = 50 Hz.
An instrument that displays how voltage changes over time; used to show the difference between AC and DC waveforms.

keyPoints.memTip: AC = Alternates, DC = Direct (one direction). The mains 'alternates'. Think of it swinging like a pendulum, back and forth 50 times a second.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often say 'AC is more dangerous than DC'. This is not strictly true. Both are dangerous at mains voltages. Focus on the engineering reason AC is used for mains: it works with transformers.

keyPoints.heading: The three-pin plug
keyPoints.content: A UK three-pin plug has three wires. Each is a different colour, and each has a specific job. The live wire (BROWN) carries the alternating voltage from the mains supply. This is the dangerous wire (230 V AC). The neutral wire (BLUE) completes the circuit and returns current to the supply. It is at about 0 V and is much safer to touch. But you should never touch any live circuit. The earth wire (GREEN and YELLOW stripes) is a safety wire. It connects the metal casing of the appliance to the ground (0 V). Normally, no current flows through the earth wire. Say a fault develops and the live wire touches the metal casing. Then the casing becomes live. But the earth wire gives a low-resistance path for the current to flow safely to earth. This large current blows the fuse. That breaks the circuit before anyone is electrocuted. The plug also has a cable grip that clamps the outer insulation. So the wires cannot be pulled loose if someone tugs the cable. Memory trick: BLue = Neutral, BRown = Live (BLaNk = Blue Neutral; BRiLliant = Brown Live).
writeBullets: Live wire — BROWN. Carries 230 V AC from the supply. The most dangerous wire
Neutral wire — BLUE. Returns current to the supply. About 0 V
Earth wire — GREEN and YELLOW. A safety wire connecting the metal casing to the ground
Earth + fuse: fault → casing goes live → large current → fuse blows → circuit broken
Cable grip — clamps the outer insulation so the wires can't be pulled loose
Memory: BLue Neutral, BRown Live

keyTerms.def: The brown wire in a UK plug; carries the 230 V AC supply voltage and is the most dangerous wire.
The blue wire; completes the circuit and returns current to the supply at approximately 0 V.
The green and yellow striped wire; a safety wire that connects the metal casing to earth, allowing fault current to flow safely and blow the fuse.
A thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit when current exceeds its rated value, protecting against overheating and fire.

keyPoints.memTip: BLue Neutral, BRown Live. Or picture a bruise. BLue = Neutral is the 'safer' one. BRown is the 'live danger' one.
keyPoints.tutor_note: A very common exam question asks why the fuse must be in the live wire. Why not the neutral wire? Say the fuse were in the neutral wire and it blew. The appliance would still be connected to 230 V. That is dangerous.

keyPoints.heading: Fuses and circuit breakers
keyPoints.content: A fuse is a thin wire inside a ceramic casing. It is connected in series with the live wire. When the current goes above the fuse's rated current, the wire heats up and melts. That breaks the circuit. Choose a fuse rating just above the normal working current. Worked example: a lamp drawing 0.2 A uses a 3 A fuse (the next standard size up). A kettle drawing 9 A uses a 13 A fuse. Common UK fuse ratings: 3 A (lamps, phone chargers, TVs), 5 A, and 13 A (kettles, irons, microwaves). If the rating is too high, the fuse won't blow when there is a fault. That is dangerous. If it is too low, it keeps blowing for no reason. Once a fuse blows, it must be replaced. A circuit breaker (MCB — miniature circuit breaker) is an electromagnetic switch in the consumer unit (fuse box). It trips and switches off when the current is too high. It can be reset by flicking the switch back. This is much easier than replacing fuses. An RCCB (residual current circuit breaker) is even more sensitive. It detects tiny differences in current between the live and neutral wires, even just 30 mA. If someone is being electrocuted, current leaks through their body instead of the neutral wire. The RCCB detects this imbalance and trips within milliseconds. This could save a life.
writeBullets: Fuse — a thin wire in series with the live wire. It melts and breaks the circuit when the current is too high
Correct fuse rating: just above the normal working current of the appliance
3 A: lamps, chargers. 13 A: kettles, irons, microwaves
Fuse too high: won't blow in a fault (dangerous). Too low: keeps blowing for no reason
MCB (circuit breaker) — a reusable electromagnetic switch. It trips and can be reset
RCCB — detects a current imbalance between live and neutral. Trips in milliseconds. Protects against electric shock

keyTerms.def: The maximum current (in amps) a fuse can carry before it melts and breaks the circuit.
Miniature circuit breaker — an electromagnetic switch in the consumer unit that trips when current is too high; can be reset unlike a fuse.
Residual current circuit breaker — detects tiny current differences between live and neutral wires; trips within milliseconds to prevent electrocution.

keyPoints.memTip: Fuse = sacrificial. It destroys itself to save you. MCB = reusable. Flick it back.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to misread what a fuse rating means. The rating is the current at which the fuse blows, not the current it allows. And fuses are always in the live wire.

keyPoints.heading: Earthing and double insulation
keyPoints.content: Earthing means connecting an appliance's metal casing to earth (0 V). This is done through the earth wire (green and yellow). Normally, no current flows through the earth wire. Say there is a fault, and the live wire inside the appliance touches the metal casing. The casing becomes live at 230 V. Without earthing, anyone touching the casing would get an electric shock. Current would flow through them to earth. With earthing: - the earth wire gives a low-resistance path - a very large current flows through the earth wire - this blows the fuse or trips the MCB - the circuit breaks before anyone is harmed The earth wire and fuse must always work together for this protection to work. Double insulation is used for appliances with fully plastic casings. Examples are hairdryers, power drills and some lamps. The casing is plastic, which is an insulator. So the live wire cannot make the casing dangerous, and no earth wire is needed. These appliances use two-core cables (live + neutral only). The double-insulation symbol is a small square inside a larger square. Electrical safety rules: - never use electrical appliances near water (water conducts electricity) - never overload sockets with adaptors - always check cables for damage before use - use the correct fuse rating
writeBullets: Earthing — connects the metal casing to earth through the green and yellow wire. Protects against electric shock
Fault sequence: live touches casing → casing goes live → large current through earth wire → fuse blows → circuit broken
Double insulation — a plastic casing cannot become live. No earth wire needed
Double-insulated appliances use two-core cable (live + neutral only)
Double insulation symbol: a small square inside a larger square
Safety rules: no appliances near water. No overloaded sockets. Check cables. Use the correct fuse

keyTerms.def: Connecting the metal casing of an appliance to earth via the earth wire, so a fault causes a large current that blows the fuse rather than electrocuting a user.
Safety feature where an appliance has a fully insulating (plastic) casing, so no earth wire is needed — used in hairdryers, power tools, etc.
A cable containing only a live and a neutral wire — used for double-insulated appliances that do not need an earth wire.

keyPoints.memTip: Earth = escape route for fault current. Double insulated = nothing to earth (no metal casing).
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to think earthing prevents faults. It doesn't. It controls what happens when a fault occurs. The earth wire gives the fault current a safe route, so the fuse blows before anyone is hurt.

0.question: What is the colour and voltage of the live wire in a UK three-pin plug?
0.correctFeedback: Correct. The live wire is brown and carries the 230 V AC mains supply. It is the most dangerous wire in the plug.
0.wrongFeedback: The live wire is BROWN and carries 230 V AC. Blue is neutral (~0 V). Green and yellow is the earth wire, also ~0 V normally.

1.question: A toaster draws 4.5 A when working normally. Which fuse should be fitted?
1.correctFeedback: Spot on. The fuse rating should be just above the normal working current. 4.5 A → the next standard size up is 5 A. A 13 A fuse would not blow in a fault at 4.5 A.
1.wrongFeedback: The fuse must be rated just above the normal current drawn. For 4.5 A, 3 A is too low: it would keep blowing. 13 A is too high: it wouldn't blow in a fault. The correct choice is 5 A.

2.question: Why does a hairdryer with a plastic casing not need an earth wire?
options: Plastic is an insulator, so the casing cannot become live even if there is a fault
The hairdryer only uses DC, so earthing is not needed
Plastic casings already have an earth wire built in
The fuse provides all the necessary protection on its own
2.correctFeedback: Exactly right. The casing is plastic, which is an insulator. It cannot become live, even if the live wire touches it. So nothing can give you a shock, and no earth wire is needed.
2.wrongFeedback: The reason is the material, not the type of current or the fuse. Plastic is an electrical insulator. Even if the live wire touches the inside of the casing, the casing itself stays safe. That is what double insulation means.

3.question: What is the frequency of the UK mains AC supply, and what does this mean?
options: 50 Hz. The current reverses direction 100 times per second (50 complete cycles)
50 Hz. The voltage changes 50 times per second
60 Hz. The same as the USA
3.correctFeedback: Perfect. 50 Hz means 50 complete cycles every second. Each cycle has the current going forward, then back. So the direction changes 100 times per second.
3.wrongFeedback: The UK mains is 50 Hz. Frequency means complete cycles per second. At 50 Hz there are 50 complete cycles (and 100 direction changes) every second. The 230 V is the voltage, not the frequency.

commonMistakes: Mixing up the live and neutral wire colours. Live is BROWN and neutral is BLUE. Many people swap these. Use BLue Neutral, BRown Live.
Thinking the earth wire carries current when working normally. It does not. Current only flows through the earth wire during a fault.
Saying the fuse should be in the neutral wire. It must always be in the LIVE wire. A fuse in the neutral wire would leave the appliance connected to 230 V, even after it blows.
Choosing a fuse rating equal to the appliance's current, rather than just above it. The rating must be just above the normal current. Then it won't trip for no reason, but will still blow in a fault.
Thinking double-insulated appliances are less safe. They are just as safe. The plastic casing cannot become live, so the earth wire is not needed rather than missing.
examTips: When explaining how earthing protects you, always give the full sequence. Fault → casing live → large current through earth → fuse blows → circuit broken. Missing any step loses marks.
If asked to compare AC and DC on an oscilloscope, describe the shapes exactly. DC is a flat horizontal line. AC is a sinusoidal (S-shaped) wave with equal peaks and troughs.
For fuse questions, always choose the rating just above the working current from the standard values given. Never choose one equal to or below the working current.
revisionCardBullets: DC: one direction only, constant voltage (batteries, cells, solar panels)
AC: current reverses direction. UK mains = 230 V, 50 Hz
AC used for mains because transformers (needed for National Grid) only work with AC
Oscilloscope: DC = flat line; AC = sinusoidal wave
Live wire: BROWN, 230 V AC. The most dangerous
Neutral wire: BLUE, ~0 V. Completes the circuit
Earth wire: GREEN and YELLOW, 0 V. Safety wire that carries fault current to blow the fuse
Fuse: in series with the live wire. Melts if the current is too high. Must be replaced
Fuse rating: just above the normal working current (3 A, 5 A or 13 A)
MCB: a reusable circuit breaker. Can be reset after tripping
RCCB: detects a current imbalance between live and neutral. Trips in milliseconds and protects against electrocution
